title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
hook: in the Gita Krishna says that among letters he is the first one, a, the sound of an open mouth
carry: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the mudras with the Gita's widest picture: hands and feet everywhere, and yet no senses at all. Did you watch someone's hands at work? Today the mouth takes over from the hands. Day one thousand forty.

Open a careful English edition of the Gita and the names start to grow small marks. A line over a letter. A dot underneath. An accent perched on an s. It is easy to skip the marks, say the word the way it looks in English, and keep going. But every one of those marks is a direction for the mouth. They're how a page of English letters carries a language that was built to be heard. This week, one alphabet, learned the way it was meant to be learned: by sound.
screen: `A LINE OVER, A DOT UNDER.` → `EVERY MARK IS A DIRECTION.` → `AN ALPHABET LEARNED BY SOUND.`

segments.voice: Start with a verse. In the tenth chapter of the Gita, Krishna names, kind by kind, where he can be found. Among rivers, the Ganga. Among trees, the sacred fig. And at verse thirty-three, in paraphrase: among letters, I am the letter a. Not a grand letter. The plainest one. The sound you make when you open your mouth and let the voice out without shaping it at all. A. That letter is where the Sanskrit alphabet begins, and the whole order is a journey from there. The vowels come first. Then the consonants, arranged not at random, but by where in the mouth they're made, moving forward from the throat toward the lips. Say the alphabet in order and the sound walks out of you. There's a second gift in that small letter. In Devanagari, the script Sanskrit is often written in today, a consonant on its own already carries a short a inside it. The letter for k is read ka. The letter for m is read ma. Unless a mark tells you otherwise, the a is there, quietly, in almost every letter on the page. So Krishna's line has a reader's meaning too: the plainest sound runs through all the others. At least one Upanishad treats pronunciation as something to be taught with care. The Taittiriya Upanishad opens a lesson by announcing it: now we will explain shiksha, the teaching of sound, and lists what that teaching covers: the letter, the pitch, the length, the effort, the evenness, the joining. That's this week. Not grammar. Not vocabulary. Just the sounds, so the names you already read can be said the way they were heard.
screen: `GITA 10.33: AMONG LETTERS, I AM A.` · `FROM THE THROAT TOWARD THE LIPS.` · `A HIDES INSIDE EVERY CONSONANT.` · `SHIKSHA: THE TEACHING OF SOUND.` · then, large: `THE PLAINEST SOUND RUNS THROUGH ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit tall, and let the jaw soften. Breathe in through the nose. On the out-breath, open the mouth a little and let a quiet sound come out with no shaping at all: a. Like the beginning of the word about. Let it last as long as the breath does, soft, not loud. Then breathe in again. Notice where the sound seems to come from: the throat, the chest, somewhere behind the mouth. Keep going, one a on each out-breath, and between them, silence. If sound isn't possible where you are, say it inwardly. The bell holds the time.
Sanskrit sounds for readers. Today, the first one: a, the open mouth, the letter Krishna names in the Gita, hidden inside almost every letter on the page.
Your line: Sanskrit sounds for readers, the alphabet in sound. Today, catch one Sanskrit name you read or hear, Rama, Shiva, karma, and listen for the a inside it. Day one thousand forty.

howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit learn the alphabet aloud, in its traditional order from vowels to consonants grouped by where the mouth makes them, often reciting it with a teacher before reading texts.
